function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It assumes you have `git`, `docker`, `kubectl` and `node` installed on the machine where you run it.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to the repo from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your local machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

> *Assumption:* The repo contains a standard Node.js app (`app.js` + `package.json`) that listens on port **3000**.

Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> If you prefer the helper function, you could call it like this (in a Python script):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint="node app.js"
)
```

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may need to create the `k8s` folder first):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Using the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          # Optional: push to Docker Hub (uncomment & set secrets)
          # echo "${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}" | docker login -u "${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}" --password-stdin
          # docker tag nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} yourdockerhubuser/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          # docker push yourdockerhubuser/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Upload Docker image as artifact (optional)
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: nodejs-welcome-image
          path: ./nodejs-welcome-${{ github.sha }}.tar
```

> **Tip:** If you want to push the image to Docker Hub, set the following repository secrets:
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME`
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD`

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
# Stage everything
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new `Dockerfile` in the repo root.
* A `k8s/deployment.yaml` file under the `k8s` folder.
* A `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file that triggers on pushes to `main`.

If you navigate to the **Actions** tab on GitHub, you should see the workflow run automatically after the push.

---

That’s it! 🎉 You now have a Dockerfile, Kubernetes deployment/service, and a CI pipeline that builds the app whenever you push to `main`.
